newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: World Bank chief wants to boost trade union ties.
newsitem.headline: World Bank chief wants to boost trade union ties.

text.p: World Bank boss James Wolfensohn, stressing the human face of his lending agency, called on Thursday for closer ties with trade unions and the International Labour Organisation (ILO) to help the world's poor.

Speaking at a news conference, Wolfensohn said the bank hoped to draw on the expertise of the ILO in the field to alleviate income disparities in developing countries suffering from social problems of poverty and inequality.
"The test will be in 12 months' or two years' time whether there is a mutual confidence build-up and whether we've done 20 or 50 projects and we've worked together and reached conclusions," he said.
He said cooperation was already there, "very real."
"We're doing projects on the labour aspects of transition and on globalisation. This is far more than words."

The World Bank, which borrows money on financial markets and lends it to developing nations at a small margin, has been criticised in the past for muscling into territory of other organisations including the ILO on labour and social security.
Some U.N. agencies also resent the fact that the bank dictates its terms to borrower countries because it has the money.
Wolfensohn said the bank was being drawn into labour issues when dealing with social problems and poverty.

"We each have a different function and somewhere along the line they have to meet....you enter into questions of labour administration and pension reform. They're legitimate areas for us to go into," he said.
"What we're doing as a matter of course now is to consult with and work with the ILO. I think there have been cases in the past when maybe we haven't."

The bank president would not be drawn into the controversy over efforts by ILO Director-General Michel Hansenne to give the United Nations agency a role in assigning a "social label" to internationally-traded goods, which have been fiercely criticised by developing countries in the body.
